headings.title: Introduction and Nutritional Requirements Across Childhood
headings.content: Dietary education forms the bedrock of preventive paediatrics. A growing child requires adequate macro and micronutrients not just to survive, but to achieve optimal cognitive, motor, and immunological development. Nutritional needs shift dramatically as a child grows from a helpless newborn dependent entirely on milk to an active toddler exploring table foods, and finally to a growing adolescent undergoing a massive growth spurt. Nurses must understand these shifting physiological demands to guide parents effectively. Unlike adults, whose nutritional focus is often maintenance and disease prevention, paediatric nutrition is fundamentally about growth velocity and organ maturation. Failure to meet nutritional demands during critical windows of development can lead to irreversible stunting and cognitive deficits.

headings.title: Infant Nutrition: Breastfeeding and Formula Feeding
headings.content:
The first six months of life require an exclusive diet of breast milk or a scientifically formulated infant formula. Breast milk remains the gold standard because it provides passive immunity via antibodies, ideal digestibility, and the exact balance of fats, proteins, and carbohydrates needed for a newborn. 

- **Exclusive Breastfeeding**: Feeding an infant only breast milk with no additional food, water, or other liquids except prescribed medicines for the first six months.
- **Formula Feeding**: Using iron-fortified commercial infant formula when breastfeeding is contraindicated, insufficient, or chosen by the mother.

A common nursing pitfall is failing to support mothers with correct positioning and latch techniques, which leads to early cessation of breastfeeding due to sore nipples or perceived insufficient milk supply.

headings.title: Complementary Feeding and Weaning
headings.content:
Around six months of age, breast milk alone can no longer satisfy an infant's growing iron and energy requirements. Complementary feeding involves introducing solid and semi-solid foods alongside continued breastfeeding. Foods must be nutrient-dense, clean, and prepared with minimal salt and sugar.

1. **First Foods**: Easily digestible, iron-rich foods such as mashed local staples like yam, plantain, or iron-fortified cereals.
2. **Texture Progression**: Moving gradually from smooth mashes to thick purees, minced foods, and finally family table foods by twelve months.
3. **Responsive Feeding**: Feeding infants directly and assisting older children, being sensitive to their hunger and fullness cues.

Parents often make the mistake of introducing watery, nutrient-poor porridges as first foods, which increases the risk of protein-energy malnutrition.

headings.title: Nutritional Needs in Toddlers and School-Age Children
headings.content: Toddlers and school-age children experience slower, steadier growth compared to infants, accompanied by a noticeable drop in appetite. This physiological deceleration often panics parents, who may resort to forced feeding or excessive snacking on sugary items. Toddlers require balanced diets rich in calcium for bone development, iron for cognitive function, and healthy fats for brain development. As children enter school age, peer influence, school meals, and marketing shape their food preferences. Nurses must educate parents on establishing structured meal and snack routines, offering varied food textures, and avoiding using sweets as rewards.

headings.title: Adolescent Nutrition and Dietary Challenges
headings.content: Adolescence brings a massive pubertal growth spurt, second only to infancy in terms of velocity. Caloric and nutrient requirements peak during these years, particularly for calcium, iron, and protein. Boys require extra energy and protein for muscle mass development, while girls need additional iron to compensate for menstrual blood loss. Unfortunately, adolescents face unique nutritional challenges. Body image insecurities can trigger eating disorders, skipping meals, or fad diets. Furthermore, peer pressure often drives increased consumption of fast food, sugary drinks, and energy-dense, nutrient-poor snacks.

headings.title: Assessment of Nutritional Status in Children
headings.content:
Evaluating a child's nutritional health requires a combination of anthropometric measurements, dietary history, clinical examination, and biochemical tests. Nurses play a frontline role in screening children during routine clinic visits.

| Assessment Method | What is Measured | Clinical Purpose |
|---|---|---|>
| Anthropometry | Weight, length/height, MUAC | Comparing against WHO growth standards |
| Clinical Exam | Skin, hair, eyes, tongue signs | Spotting vitamin and protein deficiencies |
| Dietary History | 24-hour recall, food frequency | Identifying poor nutrient intake patterns |
| Biochemical | Hemoglobin, serum proteins | Detecting subclinical anaemia or deficiencies |

A drop across major weight-for-age percentiles on a growth chart serves as an early red flag for nutritional failure long before clinical wasting becomes obvious.

headings.title: Common Paediatric Nutritional Deficiencies in Nigeria
headings.content: Malnutrition remains a major public health concern in Nigeria, manifesting in both undernutrition and emerging overnutrition. Protein-energy malnutrition presents as kwashiorkor (characterized by edema and flaky skin paint dermatosis) or marasmus (characterized by severe wasting and old-man face appearance). Micronutrient deficiencies are equally damaging. Iron deficiency anaemia impairs cognitive development and school performance. Vitamin A deficiency compromises epithelial barriers, increasing susceptibility to severe measles and respiratory infections. Iodine deficiency stunts brain development, leading to cretinism. Nurses must recognize these clinical signs early and educate communities on utilizing affordable local foods rich in these vital nutrients.

headings.title: Strategies for Effective Dietary Counselling with Parents
headings.content: Giving dietary advice requires more than handing out a pamphlet. Effective counselling must respect cultural beliefs, economic realities, and family dynamics. Nurses should use open-ended questions to assess current feeding practices rather than interrogating parents. Recommendations must focus on locally available, affordable foodstuffs rather than expensive imported items. Demonstrating how to prepare nutrient-dense local meals builds parental confidence. Finally, nurses must avoid judgmental language when addressing poor feeding habits, ensuring that sessions remain collaborative and encouraging.
